title: The Journey of French Rugby
sourceTitle: History of the France national rugby union team
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Rugby came to France in the 1870s. British merchants and students brought the sport. Schools and clubs started to play. The first national team played at the 1900 Paris Olympics. They won the gold medal. However, this team is not a main Test team today.
pages.caption: The original France XV v New Zealand, 1 January 1906, Paris

evidence.articleCaption: The original France XV v New Zealand, 1 January 1906, Paris

pages.text: France played its first ever Test match in 1906. They lost to the All Blacks. Later that year, they played England and lost again. In 1910, international matches laid the foundation for a Five Nations competition. France got their first win in 1911 against Scotland in Paris.
pages.caption: Romania versus France at the Inter-Allied Games of 1919

evidence.fileTitle: File:Stade de Colombes, 22.06.1919, jeux interalliés, rugby, match France contre Roumanie.JPG
evidence.articleCaption: Romania versus France at the Inter-Allied Games of 1919

pages.text: The team faced hard times in the 1930s. France was expelled from the Five Nations in 1932. They had to play weaker teams. Even so, they won ten games in a row. They were later invited back to the tournament before war stopped games.
pages.caption: The team that played at the 1924 Summer Olympics.

evidence.articleCaption: The team that played at the 1924 Summer Olympics.

pages.text: After the Second World War, French rugby grew strong. They shared the Five Nations title for the first time in 1954 alongside England and Wales. They also recorded their first win over New Zealand. In 1961, the French won the five nations championship outright, becoming a major success.
pages.caption: France (white) playing Scotland in 2004.

evidence.articleCaption: France (white) playing Scotland in 2004.

pages.text: In later years, France won more titles. They won their second Grand Slam in 1977. In 2000, Italy joined the tournament. It became the Six Nations. France continued to play hard against top teams from around the world.

Rugby union was introduced to France in the 1870s by British merchants and students. The sport quickly spread through schools and clubs. The national side made its early appearance at the 1900 Paris Olympics, where a French team won the gold medal by defeating Britain and Germany, though these games are not considered official Test matches.
pages.caption: The original France XV v New Zealand, 1 January 1906, Paris

evidence.articleCaption: The original France XV v New Zealand, 1 January 1906, Paris

pages.text: On January 1, 1906, France played its first official Test match, losing against the All Blacks. Matches against England and other nations soon followed. By 1910, the foundation of the Five Nations competition was laid when Scotland played France, leading to France's first tournament win against Scotland in 1911.
pages.caption: Romania versus France at the Inter-Allied Games of 1919

evidence.fileTitle: File:Stade de Colombes, 22.06.1919, jeux interalliés, rugby, match France contre Roumanie.JPG
evidence.articleCaption: Romania versus France at the Inter-Allied Games of 1919

pages.text: Despite periods of improvement, France faced a major setback in 1932 when they were expelled from the Five Nations amid accusations of professionalism and on-field violence. Forced to play weaker opposition, they surprisingly won ten consecutive games. International rugby was eventually suspended due to the Second World War.
pages.caption: The team that played at the 1924 Summer Olympics.

evidence.articleCaption: The team that played at the 1924 Summer Olympics.

pages.text: The Five Nations resumed after the war in 1947, marking a new era for French rugby. Lucien Mias introduced innovative line-out tactics. France claimed a share of the Five Nations title in 1954 and secured their first victory over New Zealand. By 1961, they won the championship outright.
pages.caption: France (white) playing Scotland in 2004.

evidence.articleCaption: France (white) playing Scotland in 2004.

pages.text: The success continued into the 1970s and 1980s under figures like coach Jacques Fouroux, securing Grand Slams and memorable victories against Southern Hemisphere teams. In 2000, Italy joined the competition, transforming the Five Nations into the Six Nations, where France remained a major competitor.

pages.text: Political and administrative turmoil culminated in France's expulsion from the Five Nations in 1932 due to allegations of professionalism, violence, and poor organisation. Relegated to competing against alternative opposition, the squad assembled a ten-game winning streak before international competition was suspended upon the outbreak of the Second World War.

pages.text: The resumption of the Five Nations in 1947 catalyzed a renaissance in French rugby. Tactical innovations spearheaded by captain Lucien Mias revolutionized forward play. France achieved a shared championship title in 1954 alongside historic victories against New Zealand, eventually capturing the tournament outright in 1961.

pages.text: Subsequent decades cemented France's status as an elite rugby nation, punctuated by multiple Grand Slams under coach Jacques Fouroux and notable victories against southern hemisphere powerhouses. The inclusion of Italy in 2000 expanded the tournament into the Six Nations, marking a new chapter in the team's storied history.

title: Protecting Japan's Cultural Properties
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Japan protects many old and special things. The government has rules to keep these important items safe. They include old buildings, art, crafts, and nature. People call them Cultural Properties. The main goal is to save them for everyone to see and learn.
pages.caption: Himeji Castle's keep, designated a National Treasure in 1951(UNESCO World Heritage Site)

evidence.articleCaption: Himeji Castle's keep, designated a National Treasure in 1951(UNESCO World Heritage Site)

pages.text: There is a special system to name these important things. Items can be chosen at national, regional, or local levels. When an item gets chosen, there are strict rules. People cannot easily change, fix, or send these objects out of the country.
pages.caption: Kyūshū's Karatsu Kunchi festival was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 1980.

evidence.articleCaption: Kyūshū's Karatsu Kunchi festival was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 1980.

pages.text: Tangible Cultural Properties are real objects made by people. They include old shrines, temples, paintings, sculptures, and ancient documents. Many of these things are made of wood and can easily catch fire. Owners get help to stop fires.
pages.caption: The city of Uji near Kyoto is an Important Cultural Landscape.

evidence.articleCaption: The city of Uji near Kyoto is an Important Cultural Landscape.

pages.text: Japan also protects intangible things like music, dance, and special craft skills. Folk items, traditional ways of life, beautiful nature, and old group buildings are part of this big system. Everything helps people understand history and daily life traditions.
pages.caption: Okakura Kakuzō

evidence.articleCaption: Okakura Kakuzō

pages.text: Long ago, many temples and old buildings were lost during big political changes and modern times. Later, the government started making laws to save historic art and architecture. Today, thousands of sites and objects are carefully protected across the country.

Japan administers its rich cultural heritage through the Agency for Cultural Affairs. This diverse collection includes tangible structures, artworks, intangible performing arts, folk traditions, historic monuments, and cultural landscapes. These properties are preserved and utilized as the collective heritage of the Japanese people.
pages.caption: Himeji Castle's keep, designated a National Treasure in 1951(UNESCO World Heritage Site)

evidence.articleCaption: Himeji Castle's keep, designated a National Treasure in 1951(UNESCO World Heritage Site)

pages.text: To safeguard these assets, the Law for the Protection of Cultural Properties establishes a designation system operating at national, prefectural, and municipal levels. Designated objects face strict restrictions regarding alteration, repair, and export. A separate registration system also provides a more modest level of protection and support.
pages.caption: Kyūshū's Karatsu Kunchi festival was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 1980.

evidence.articleCaption: Kyūshū's Karatsu Kunchi festival was designated an Important Intangible Folk Cultural Property in 1980.

pages.text: Tangible cultural properties encompass physical items of high historical or artistic value, ranging from ancient architecture to fine arts and crafts. Because many of these traditional structures consist of flammable materials like wood and bark, owners receive government subsidies to install essential fire and disaster prevention systems.
pages.caption: The city of Uji near Kyoto is an Important Cultural Landscape.

evidence.articleCaption: The city of Uji near Kyoto is an Important Cultural Landscape.

pages.text: Beyond tangible objects, the protective framework covers intangible craft techniques, folk customs, scenic monuments, cultural landscapes, and groups of traditional buildings. Together, these categories preserve the physical and traditional lifestyle elements that define Japan's historical environment.
pages.caption: Okakura Kakuzō

evidence.articleCaption: Okakura Kakuzō

pages.text: The modern preservation system evolved from historical challenges. Following the Meiji Restoration and the separation of Shinto and Buddhism, numerous temples and artworks suffered destruction or neglect. In response, late 19th-century legislation and subsequent laws began systematically funding restoration and safeguarding historic architecture across the country.

pages.text: Administered by the Agency for Cultural Affairs, Japan's cultural property framework encompasses a broad spectrum of tangible assets, intangible practices, folk traditions, historic monuments, cultural landscapes, and traditional building groups. These diverse elements are legally mandated to be preserved and utilized as the heritage of the populace.

pages.text: The statutory foundation relies primarily on a designation system across national, prefectural, and municipal tiers, imposing stringent regulatory controls over alteration, repair, and exportation. A supplementary registration system offers lower-tier protection, relying on notification and guidance to encourage voluntary stewardship by property owners.

title: Understanding Deathcare Practices
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: Deathcare is the planning and work that happens after someone dies. It includes services, products, and rules. Many people help with this care. Families, doctors, and religious workers all take part in different ways.
pages.caption: Utensils used for embalming.

evidence.articleCaption: Utensils used for embalming.

pages.text: Long ago, families took care of their dead relatives at home. Women in the family usually cleaned and dressed bodies. Later, the American Civil War changed things. Soldiers died far from home, so people started using embalming to save bodies.
pages.caption: Cremation rituals at Manikarnika Ghat, Varanasi, India, one of the most significant Hindu cremation sites.

evidence.articleCaption: Cremation rituals at Manikarnika Ghat, Varanasi, India, one of the most significant Hindu cremation sites.

pages.text: After the war, morticians began preparing bodies for families. Funeral homes became common places for services. Today, the deathcare industry has three main parts. These parts are ceremonies, disposition of remains, and memorial art or monuments.
pages.caption: Hindu funeral ritual/ceremony.

imageProvenance.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author Unknown authorUnknown author

evidence.articleCaption: Hindu funeral ritual/ceremony.

pages.text: Traditional burials and cremations can harm the environment. Metal caskets can pollute soil and water. Cremation uses a lot of fuel and creates air pollution. Because of this, new methods like human composting are growing.
pages.caption: Mortality rate of COVID-19.

evidence.articleCaption: Mortality rate of COVID-19.

pages.text: Governments make laws for deathcare. They decide what practices and organizations are allowed. Private companies, religious groups, and non-government organizations also help shape deathcare policies around the world today.

Deathcare encompasses the planning, provision, and governance of post-death services. The timeline following clinical death involves immediate medical professionals, followed by a diverse course shaped by cultural, religious, and personal traditions involving numerous types of workers.
pages.caption: Utensils used for embalming.

evidence.articleCaption: Utensils used for embalming.

pages.text: Historically, deathcare was decentralized and largely managed by families. Women typically oversaw the preparation and burial of relatives at home. However, the high mortality of the American Civil War popularized embalming to preserve fallen soldiers for transport back home.
pages.caption: Cremation rituals at Manikarnika Ghat, Varanasi, India, one of the most significant Hindu cremation sites.

evidence.articleCaption: Cremation rituals at Manikarnika Ghat, Varanasi, India, one of the most significant Hindu cremation sites.

pages.text: Following the war, professional morticians and funeral homes became the norm for caring for the deceased. Analysts divide the modern deathcare industry into three parts: ceremonies, disposition through burial or cremation, and memorialization.

pages.text: Traditional practices carry environmental costs. Conventional burials using metal caskets can contaminate soil and groundwater, while cremation consumes significant fuel and generates greenhouse gas emissions. These concerns have driven interest in sustainable alternatives like human composting.

pages.text: Governments establish the legal frameworks governing deathcare, though religious, private, and third-sector organizations also shape these policies. Meanwhile, the global deathcare market has shown substantial fiscal growth, driven by an expanding demand for services and products.

Deathcare functions simultaneously as an industry of practitioners, a domain of public policy, and an interdisciplinary academic field. From the moment of clinical death, a diverse timeline unfolds, engaging immediate medical personnel alongside cultural, religious, and community figures.

The American Civil War catalyzed a shift toward preservation, as widespread fatalities necessitated embalming to facilitate the long-distance transport of soldiers.

title: The History and Structure of Parties
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: A political party is a group that helps candidates run in elections and take part in government. Most countries have political parties. They are a big part of politics in both democracies and autocracies today.
pages.caption: In A Block for the Wigs (1783), James Gillray caricatured Fox's return to power in a coalition with North. George III is the blockhead in the centre.

title: Seeking Peace Through Cameroon's Dialogue
attribution: Adapted from English Wikipedia contributors; see pinned revision and history. SAGA AI-assisted adaptation under CC BY-SA 4.0. Wikipedia does not endorse SAGA.

pages.text: The Major National Dialogue was a meeting between the Government of Cameroon and different opposition parties. The goal was to find a way to solve the Anglophone Crisis. The event took place from September 30 to October 4, 2019.
pages.caption: Joseph Dion Ngute, Prime Minister of Cameroon, visits the plenary hall of the Palais des Congrès in Yaoundé on Sept. 29, 2019, on the eve of the Major National Dialogue.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Nguté visité la Palais des congrès.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Joseph Dion Ngute, Prime Minister of Cameroon, visits the plenary hall of the Palais des Congrès in Yaoundé on Sept. 29, 2019, on the eve of the Major National Dialogue.

pages.text: For many years, English-speaking people in the former Southern Cameroons felt ignored by the central government. Protests started in October 2016. Soldiers were sent to stop the protests. Soon, people were killed and arrested.

By September 2017, separatists began to fight the government with weapons. They declared the independence of a new region. This conflict became known as the Anglophone Crisis, which involved serious human rights violations.

In September 2019, President Paul Biya announced that a big national dialogue would happen. The talks had to follow the constitution, meaning independence was not allowed. People could also send proposals on a website.

The meeting started with an opening ceremony where former fighters sang the national anthem. Prime Minister Joseph Ngute told the attendants to make history and find solutions to the problems that divided them.

On the final day, the commissions shared their recommendations. They proposed a special status and more local autonomy for the English-speaking regions. However, the conflict continued to grow after the event ended.

The Major National Dialogue was an official meeting held between the Government of Cameroon and various opposition parties. Its main aim was to resolve the ongoing Anglophone Crisis, taking place from September 30 to October 4, 2019.
pages.caption: Joseph Dion Ngute, Prime Minister of Cameroon, visits the plenary hall of the Palais des Congrès in Yaoundé on Sept. 29, 2019, on the eve of the Major National Dialogue.

evidence.fileTitle: File:Nguté visité la Palais des congrès.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Joseph Dion Ngute, Prime Minister of Cameroon, visits the plenary hall of the Palais des Congrès in Yaoundé on Sept. 29, 2019, on the eve of the Major National Dialogue.

pages.text: Decades of resentment over perceived marginalization by the central government led to major protests in the Anglophone regions in October 2016. The government deployed soldiers to quell the demonstrations, resulting in deaths and numerous arrests. Separatists took up arms by September 2017 and declared independence, turning the situation into a violent conflict.

President Paul Biya announced the upcoming dialogue in a televised speech, stating it would remain within the constitutional framework, thereby ruling out independence. Citizens submitted proposals via a newly launched government website ahead of the event.

The event opened with former separatist fighters singing the national anthem, followed by Prime Minister Joseph Ngute challenging attendants to find solutions to the divisions of recent years. Eight different commissions were established to focus on specific issues like bilingualism, the judicial system, and decentralization.

On the final day, the commissions submitted their recommendations. Proposals included a special status and local autonomy for the Anglophone regions, anti-corruption measures, and the rehabilitation of former fighters. President Biya also dropped court cases against hundreds of activists.

Reactions to the dialogue were mixed. While the ruling party welcomed the outcome, critics and separatists dismissed the event, promising to escalate the war. Despite subsequent legislation granting special status, the conflict in the regions intensified.

pages.text: The Major National Dialogue convened between September 30 and October 4, 2019, representing an official initiative between the Government of Cameroon and diverse opposition factions to address the multifaceted Anglophone Crisis.
pages.caption: Joseph Dion Ngute, Prime Minister of Cameroon, visits the plenary hall of the Palais des Congrès in Yaoundé on Sept. 29, 2019, on the eve of the Major National Dialogue.

pages.text: Historical grievances regarding the marginalization of Anglophone Cameroonians escalated into widespread protests in October 2016. The subsequent deployment of state security forces and subsequent casualties catalyzed an armed separatist movement in September 2017, culminating in a declaration of independence and sustained conflict characterized by human rights violations.

President Paul Biya announced the summit in September 2019, explicitly stipulating that proceedings would adhere strictly to the constitution, thereby excluding secessionist aspirations. A dedicated portal was established to harvest citizen proposals.

Deliberations commenced with an inaugural ceremony featuring former combatants, followed by Prime Minister Joseph Ngute urging delegates to bridge institutional divides. Eight specialized commissions were subsequently constituted to evaluate domains ranging from decentralization to the educational framework.

As the dialogue drew to a close, commissions delivered extensive recommendations, including special administrative status and augmented autonomy for the Northwest and Southwest regions. Concurrently, President Biya discontinued legal proceedings against numerous activists.

While legislative bodies subsequently codified special status provisions through the General Code of Regional and Local Authorities, outcomes remained contentious. Separatist factions repudiated the dialogue entirely, and regional hostilities intensified despite international appeals for continued engagement.

title: How the Microscope Revealed the Invisible

pages.text: A microscope is a tool used to see very small things. These objects are too small for human eyes to see. People use microscopes to study tiny things in science and medicine.
pages.caption: 18th-century microscopes from the Musée des Arts et Métiers, Paris

evidence.articleCaption: 18th-century microscopes from the Musée des Arts et Métiers, Paris

pages.text: The first simple microscopes were magnifying glasses. People started using them in the thirteenth century with eyeglasses. Later, compound microscopes appeared in Europe around sixteen twenty. The true inventor remains unknown today.
pages.caption: A stand microscope created by Joseph Gutteridge in the 1860s, held in the collection of the Herbert Art Gallery and Museum

evidence.articleCaption: A stand microscope created by Joseph Gutteridge in the 1860s, held in the collection of the Herbert Art Gallery and Museum

pages.text: In the seventeenth century, naturalists began studying biology with microscopes. Robert Hooke and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made famous discoveries. Leeuwenhoek achieved high magnification using a single small glass ball lens.

pages.text: A microscope is a laboratory instrument designed to examine objects that are too small for the naked eye. Microscopy is the science of investigating these tiny structures, which remain invisible without optical or scientific aid.
pages.caption: 18th-century microscopes from the Musée des Arts et Métiers, Paris

evidence.articleCaption: 18th-century microscopes from the Musée des Arts et Métiers, Paris

pages.text: Although early magnifying glasses date back centuries, compound microscopes first appeared in Europe around 1620. The exact inventor is still unknown despite various historical claims involving Dutch spectacle makers and Cornelius Drebbel. Galileo Galilei also built an improved version after experimenting with his telescope.
pages.caption: A stand microscope created by Joseph Gutteridge in the 1860s, held in the collection of the Herbert Art Gallery and Museum

evidence.articleCaption: A stand microscope created by Joseph Gutteridge in the 1860s, held in the collection of the Herbert Art Gallery and Museum

pages.text: During the 1660s and 1670s, naturalists began using these instruments for serious biological study. Robert Hooke published impressive illustrations in his 1665 book Micrographia. Meanwhile, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used single-lens microscopes to achieve high magnification, eventually discovering micro-organisms and red blood cells.
pages.caption: Carl Zeiss binocular compound microscope, 1914

pages.text: A significant technological shift occurred in the early twentieth century with the invention of the electron microscope. Developed by Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll, this device uses a beam of electrons and electromagnets instead of light and glass lenses, allowing for a much higher resolution.

pages.text: Modern research has continued to push the boundaries of imaging technology. Scientists developed scanning probe microscopes based on quantum tunneling, as well as fluorescence microscopes that analyze cellular structures with targeted chemical stains.

Contemporary developments include super-resolution optical techniques and X-ray instruments used in tomography. These diverse tools allow researchers to examine biological materials and material defects with unprecedented precision across various scientific fields.

Microscopy encompasses the scientific investigation of structures and objects imperceptible to the unaided human eye. Instruments utilized for this purpose interact with samples via light, electrons, photon emissions, or scanning probes to produce observable analytical images.

pages.text: The twentieth century yielded major alternatives to conventional light optics. Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll developed the transmission electron microscope, substituting electromagnetic lenses and electron beams for glass and light to surmount traditional optical resolution limitations.

pages.text: Subsequent innovations expanded analytical capabilities further. Gerd Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer engineered scanning probe microscopes based on quantum tunneling phenomena, while late-twentieth-century advancements in fluorescence microscopy enabled molecular-level cellular analysis through targeted fluorophores.

Current research focuses on super-resolution techniques, such as stimulated emission depletion microscopy, which approach electron microscope resolution thresholds. Concurrently, X-ray instruments and acoustic microscopes provide specialized three-dimensional tomographic and subsurface imaging across diverse scientific disciplines.
